notes: Each eval targets specific non-negotiables and references. Assertions are written to be checkable by a grader (LLM or human) against the model's output. 'prog' assertions are also checkable programmatically by scripts/grade_programmatic.py against with-skill Godot/code outputs. Baseline = no skill.

Uses asymmetric gravity (falls faster than it rises)
Uses CharacterBody2D + move_and_slide (kinematic), not a RigidBody for the avatar

evals.name: scope-finish-deckbuilder

Gives concrete scope-cutting discipline (treat features as costs, cut list, define 'done', one core mechanic)
Defines a concrete finishable 'done' target for a small first version
Names the hidden iceberg work (menus/save/options) and/or recommends timeboxing

evals.name: engine-select-python-cozy-sim

Does NOT reflexively default to Unity without justification
Recommends data-driven design (crops/machines/recipes as data/Resources, not hardcoded) for a sim
Injects scope realism for a first commercial sim project (start small, prove the loop)

evals.name: game-feel-diagnosis
evals.prompt: My 2D action game (Unity) technically works but it feels lifeless and floaty, and hitting enemies has no impact. What can I do?

assertions.text: Recommends hitstop/hitlag (brief freeze on impact) to sell hits
Recommends screenshake (ideally trauma-based) on impacts
Recommends particles/flash on hits (sparks, hit flash, debris)
Recommends sound on impactful actions / pitch variation
Addresses 'floaty' with movement feel (asymmetric gravity, acceleration, tighter control) not just visuals
Recommends tweening/easing and/or squash-stretch instead of instant snaps
Mentions knockback/recoil to convey impact
Gives Unity-specific levers (Time.timeScale for hitstop, Cinemachine/impulse for shake, DOTween/coroutines) where relevant
Advises restraint/accessibility (don't overdo shake; reduce-motion option) rather than maxing every effect

evals.name: enemy-horde-pathing
evals.prompt: I'm making a survivors-like in Godot 4. I've got a few hundred enemies that all chase the player, but they bunch up into a single blob on top of each other and the framerate tanks. How should I handle their movement and pathfinding?

assertions.text: Recommends a flow field / vector-field (Dijkstra-map) pathing shared by all agents instead of per-enemy A*
Explicitly warns against running A*/pathfinding per enemy per frame for hundreds of agents
Recommends separation steering (boids-style) to stop enemies stacking into one blob
Backs 'nearby enemies' queries with a spatial grid/hash, not an all-pairs scan
Mentions time-slicing/LOD AI and/or pooling for the many-agent performance problem
Keeps movement frame-independent (fixed step / delta)
Recomputes the field on goal movement/timer, not naively every frame for every agent

evals.name: procgen-dungeon-validate
evals.prompt: Help me write procedural level generation for my roguelike — rooms connected by corridors. A couple of my generated levels have had the exit walled off in an unreachable area, which is a disaster. How should I approach this?

assertions.text: Centers the fix on generate-then-validate: flood-fill/reachability check from start to exit, regenerate or patch if invalid
Recommends seeding the RNG (reproducible runs, debuggable, shareable seeds)
Recommends a concrete generation technique (room placement+corridors, BSP, etc.) appropriate to the ask
Addresses connectivity guarantee (carve connecting corridor / ensure spanning connectivity), not just detection
Mentions controlled randomness or constraints where relevant (spacing, validity rules) rather than pure uniform random
Does not hand back unseeded, unvalidated generation that could still softlock

evals.name: framerate-dependent-debug
evals.prompt:
Players keep telling me my game runs way faster on their gaming PC than on my older laptop, and it's unplayable on fast machines. I can't figure out why. Here's my movement code:

```gdscript
func _process(delta):
    if Input.is_action_pressed("right"):
        position.x += 5
    if Input.is_action_pressed("left"):
        position.x -= 5
    velocity.y += 1
    position.y += velocity.y
```

What's going on?

assertions.text: Correctly diagnoses framerate dependence: speeds are per-frame, so more FPS = faster movement
Fixes movement to be per-second by multiplying by delta (e.g. 300 * delta), not per-frame constants
Notes gravity/velocity integration is also framerate-dependent and must use delta
Recommends moving physics/movement to _physics_process (fixed timestep) rather than _process
Explains the concept (frame independence) so the user can avoid it elsewhere, not just patches the snippet

Identifies that 'velocity.y += 1; position.y += velocity.y' is doubly framerate-dependent: velocity itself grows proportionally with FPS, making gravity quadratically worse at high framerates (not just linearly faster)

evals.name: survivors-collision-love
evals.prompt: I'm building a survivors-like in LÖVE and I need the core collision/update systems to handle hundreds of projectiles against hundreds of enemies without the framerate dying. Just write me the core systems — the spatial structure and how projectiles check against enemies — I'll wire up rendering and spawning myself.

assertions.text: Implements a spatial hash/grid for the broad phase rather than checking all pairs
Projectiles query only nearby cells, not every enemy (avoids O(n^2))
Uses object pooling / instance reuse instead of allocating and collecting every frame
Movement and timers are frame-independent (multiplied by dt)
Uses LÖVE idioms correctly (love.update(dt), tables as entities)
No nested all-pairs loop over every entity against every other entity
Code is correct and runnable (valid Lua, coherent narrow-phase overlap test)

evals.name: camera-lerp-framerate-trap
evals.prompt:
I'm writing a smooth camera follow in Godot 4 and it feels different on different machines — buttery smooth on my desktop but sluggish and slow on my laptop. Here's my code:

```gdscript
func _process(delta):
    position = position.lerp(target.global_position, 0.1)
```

What's wrong and how do I fix it properly?

assertions.text: Correctly diagnoses that lerp(a, b, 0.1) per frame is framerate-dependent — higher FPS means the camera catches up faster
Does NOT suggest the naive fix of multiplying the lerp weight by delta (e.g. 0.1 * delta) — that is mathematically wrong and produces different convergence
Provides the correct framerate-independent formula: lerp(a, b, 1.0 - pow(decay, delta)) where decay is the fraction remaining per second, or equivalent exponential decay
Explains WHY the exponential form is correct (lerp each frame compounds multiplicatively, so the right delta correction is an exponent, not a multiplication)
Either uses the exponential decay formula in _process OR recommends moving to _physics_process (fixed timestep) as an alternative that sidesteps the issue

evals.name: rigidbody-avatar-trap

assertions.text: Identifies the root cause as using RigidBody2D (physics simulation) instead of a kinematic controller
Recommends switching the architecture to CharacterBody2D + move_and_slide rather than just tuning RigidBody parameters
Explains why RigidBody is wrong for precise avatar control (fighting the physics engine, forces-based motion is hard to author, non-deterministic feel)
Does NOT primarily suggest tuning RigidBody properties (linear_damp, angular_damp, physics material, mass) as the main fix
Mentions at least one feel improvement beyond the architecture switch (coyote time, jump buffer, asymmetric gravity, or Input Map)

evals.name: ecs-small-game-trap
evals.prompt: I'm starting a new 2D roguelike with about 20 enemy types. I keep reading that ECS (Entity-Component-System) is the professional approach for game development. Should I build my game on an ECS architecture? I don't want to paint myself into a corner.

assertions.text: Does NOT blindly recommend a full ECS framework for a 20-enemy-type roguelike
Explains when ECS actually earns its overhead (10k+ entities with cache-sensitive simulation, e.g. factory sims, colony builders, custom physics) — not a 20-enemy roguelike
Recommends an appropriate level of composition for this scale: Godot nodes as components, plain data tables, or simple component bags — without a heavy ECS framework
Names real costs of full ECS frameworks at small scale: cognitive overhead, tooling complexity, debugging difficulty, integration friction with engine features
Does NOT imply that using Godot/Unity node composition is an architectural mistake or inferior to ECS for this scope

evals.name: hitstop-priority-trap
evals.prompt: I've added particle explosion effects, four different hit sound variations, and screen shake to my attacks in my 2D action game. The attacks still feel weak and unsatisfying — enemies just take damage numbers but there's no sense of impact. I've spent weeks on visual effects. What am I still missing?

assertions.text: Identifies hitstop/hitlag (brief freeze on impact) as the most likely missing element, given that particles and sound are already present
Explains WHY hitstop is the highest-ROI impact technique: it's what makes the brain register a hit as 'landed' — a brief freeze sells force in a way no amount of particles can
Does NOT primarily recommend adding more particles, more sounds, or stronger screenshake as the main fix
Gives concrete hitstop implementation guidance (2–8 frames / 30–130 ms, Time.timeScale = 0 or skipping sim steps, scale with hit weight)
Explains the stacking principle: hitstop + flash + screenshake + sound together create impact where any single element alone is underwhelming

evals.name: godot-autoload-overuse
evals.prompt: I'm organizing my Godot 4 project and I've set up these autoloads (singletons): GameManager, UIManager, AudioManager, EnemyManager, PlayerManager, InventoryManager, SaveManager, and EventBus. Everything is wired through these. Is this a solid architecture for a solo indie game?

assertions.text: Identifies this pattern as autoload overuse / too many global singletons for a solo indie game
Explains specific problems: hidden dependencies between systems, initialization order fragility, singletons that accumulate unrelated state, difficulty isolating and testing scenes
Recommends EventBus (or 1–2 utilities like AudioManager or SaveManager) as the only well-justified autoloads — not a manager for every system
Recommends moving most logic into scenes/nodes that own their state, using signals to communicate upward and across
Does NOT validate all 8 autoloads as a good or neutral pattern

evals.name: pixel-perfect-setup
evals.prompt: I'm making a pixel art game in Godot 4, inspired by games like Stardew Valley and the original Legend of Zelda. When I run my game, all my sprites look blurry — the pixel edges are soft instead of crisp. How do I fix this and set up the project correctly for pixel art?

assertions.text: Instructs the user to change the texture filter to Nearest (no filter / point sampling) — specifically via Project Settings → Rendering → Textures → Canvas Textures → Default Texture Filter → Nearest (or equivalent), NOT bilinear/linear

Addresses viewport scaling: set Stretch Mode to 'canvas_items' (or 'viewport') with a small base resolution (e.g. 320×180) so the game upscales at an integer factor — NOT just making the window larger without fixing the filter
Explains WHY blurring happens: the default bilinear filter interpolates between adjacent pixels when scaling, which smooths pixel edges; Nearest-neighbor takes the closest pixel instead
Mentions that individual sprite textures may also need their import filter set to Nearest if they were imported before the project default was changed
Does NOT recommend using a fractional scale factor (e.g. 1.5× or 2.7×) — integer scaling is required to keep all pixels the same on-screen size
Optionally mentions snapping the camera position to integers each frame to prevent sub-pixel shimmer during scrolling

evals.name: zelda-topdown-grid
evals.prompt: I'm building a top-down action RPG in Godot 4 — like the original Legend of Zelda. How should I handle the grid-based world, player movement, and collision? I want it to feel like the classic game where movement is 4-directional and the world is tile-based.

assertions.text: Uses CharacterBody2D (kinematic) for the player, NOT RigidBody2D
Recommends or describes a TileMap node for the tile-based world (with collision shapes on wall/obstacle tiles via TileSet)
Explains or implements 4-directional movement (cardinal directions only) — preferring one axis over the other when diagonal input is given, matching classic Zelda behavior
Addresses how to drive the animation from the facing/velocity direction (last non-zero direction) so the sprite keeps facing the last direction when standing still

For grid-locked movement: describes animating the visual position with a tween while the logical grid position updates instantly (so collision logic is tile-coordinate based but movement looks smooth)
Mentions collision/physics layers to separate player, enemies, and environment tiles
Does NOT suggest a 3D approach or overcomplicate the architecture beyond what a classic top-down 2D game needs

evals.name: 3d-character-controller
evals.prompt: I'm making a 3D platformer in Godot 4 — think Super Mario 64 style. How do I build a character controller that actually feels tight and responsive? My previous attempt using RigidBody3D was floaty and the physics felt like I was fighting the engine.

assertions.text: Recommends switching from RigidBody3D to CharacterBody3D + move_and_slide() — explains WHY RigidBody is wrong for avatar control (fighting the physics engine, forces-based = hard to author, non-deterministic feel)
Puts physics in _physics_process (fixed timestep, NOT _process)
Applies gravity manually using velocity.y -= gravity * delta (or get_gravity()), NOT relying on the physics engine to apply it
Implements camera-relative horizontal movement: rotates the raw input vector by the camera pivot's Y rotation (basis) so the player moves relative to where the camera is facing
Uses acceleration and deceleration (move_toward) on horizontal velocity rather than snapping instantly to max speed
Exposes feel constants as @export tunables (speed, jump_velocity, acceleration, etc.)
Suggests at least one platformer feel technique for 3D (coyote time, jump buffer, variable jump height, or asymmetric fall gravity)

evals.name: 3d-camera-springarm
evals.prompt: I'm building a third-person 3D game in Godot 4. My camera keeps clipping through walls — when I walk near a wall or into a corner, the camera goes inside the geometry. Also, how should I handle the camera rotation so it orbits around the player properly with mouse input?

assertions.text: Recommends SpringArm3D as the solution to wall clipping — explains that it auto-shortens when geometry is between the camera and pivot, eliminating clip without manual raycasting
Describes the correct node hierarchy: Player → CameraPivot (Node3D) → SpringArm3D → Camera3D — NOT Camera3D as a direct child of the player
Rotates the CameraPivot (not the Camera3D directly) based on mouse motion — horizontal mouse → CameraPivot.rotate_y(), vertical mouse → CameraPivot.rotation.x with clamping
Clamps vertical (pitch) rotation to prevent gimbal flip (e.g. -60° to 80°)
Notes that SpringArm3D's collision mask should include the environment/world layer (so walls shorten the arm) but NOT the player or enemy layers (so the arm doesn't shorten due to nearby actors)
Does NOT suggest manually raycasting from pivot to camera and repositioning the camera as the primary solution — SpringArm3D handles this
Does NOT suggest parenting Camera3D directly to the CharacterBody3D as a good approach — that produces a fixed angle with no clip protection

evals.name: status-effects-design
evals.prompt: I'm building a JRPG in Godot 4. I need to implement status effects — things like Poison, Paralysis, Burn, and Berserk. How should I structure this system? I want to be able to stack some effects, have them tick each turn, and easily add new ones without touching existing code.

assertions.text: Recommends a data-driven or component-based approach where each effect is a Resource/class with defined methods (enter/tick/exit or apply/remove) rather than a hardcoded if-elif chain in the combat loop

Defines a clear effect contract — each status effect knows what it does on application, each tick, and on removal — so new effects are authored as new data/classes, not by modifying existing combat code

Addresses stacking policy as per-effect configuration: some effects replace (paralysis), some stack additively (poison instances), some cap at N — this decision belongs in the effect data, not hardcoded in a central manager

Separates effect definition (what the effect does, its duration) from effect instance state (who has it, remaining ticks) — the same StatusEffectData resource/class can be shared; per-entity state is tracked separately
Implements the tick loop by iterating the entity's active_effects list and calling each effect's tick method — NOT a giant if/elif chain checking named effects by string or enum

Does NOT implement the system as a collection of boolean flags on the entity (is_poisoned: bool, is_paralyzed: bool, is_burned: bool) — this pattern cannot be extended without modifying the entity class for every new effect

evals.name: inventory-equipment-data
evals.prompt: I'm designing an inventory and equipment system for an action-RPG in Godot 4 — like Zelda or a roguelike. Players can pick up items, equip weapons and armor, and see their stats change. How should I architect this so it's data-driven and easy to extend with new items?

assertions.text: Represents items as data resources (Godot Resource subclass or equivalent ScriptableObject pattern) — item definitions are authored as data assets, not hardcoded classes per item type
Separates item definition (ItemData: name, icon, stats, slot type) from item instance (a runtime wrapper holding the ItemData reference plus quantity, durability, or enchantments)
Equipment slots are typed (dict keyed by an enum or typed array of EquipmentSlot) — not a list of booleans or untyped strings. Equipping an item checks slot compatibility and swaps correctly.

Stat modifiers use an additive+multiplicative pattern (base_stat * (1 + sum_of_additive_bonuses) * product_of_multipliers) or a modifier list rather than recomputing from scratch with custom logic per item
Emits a signal/event on equip and unequip so the HUD and stat display update reactively — the inventory does NOT reach directly into HUD nodes to update labels
Does NOT hardcode item effects as if/elif chains by item name or ID (e.g. 'if item.name == Sword: damage += 5') — item stat contributions come from the item's data

evals.name: audio-bus-hierarchy
evals.prompt: My game needs working volume sliders for Music, SFX, and a Master volume — and players should be able to mute each category independently. How do I set this up properly in Godot 4, and what else should I know about organizing game audio?

assertions.text: Instructs setting up an Audio Bus Layout with multiple named buses (Master, Music, SFX at minimum) — NOT routing all sounds through the single default Master bus
Explains that AudioStreamPlayer/2D/3D nodes connect to the appropriate bus via the 'bus' property — so music players go to the Music bus, SFX players to the SFX bus, etc.
Volume sliders call AudioServer.set_bus_volume_db(bus_index, linear_to_db(value)) — NOT setting volume_db on individual AudioStreamPlayer nodes, which would require tracking every player instance
Uses linear_to_db() (or the equivalent dB conversion) when converting slider values to bus volume — a direct linear mapping produces perceptually wrong volume response
Muting a category uses AudioServer.set_bus_mute(bus_index, true/false) — enabling per-category mute independently of volume
Does NOT recommend a single AudioManager that plays all sounds from one shared AudioStreamPlayer — this prevents per-category volume and mute control and can only play one sound at a time

evals.name: adaptive-music
evals.prompt: I want my game's music to react to gameplay — peaceful ambient music when exploring, tense music during combat, and a dramatic sting when the boss appears. How do I implement adaptive or dynamic music in Godot 4?

assertions.text: Recommends a stem/layer approach: multiple AudioStreamPlayers all looping synchronized stems (e.g. exploration_base, exploration_melody, combat_drums, combat_strings) with volume faded in/out per state — NOT stopping one track and starting another, which causes silence gaps and sync loss
Synchronizes stems by matching playback_position: when adding a new stem, set its playback_position to match a currently playing stem before calling play(), so all stems stay in sync
Uses a state machine (e.g. Exploration / Combat / BossFight) to drive which stems are audible — state transitions tween the volume of the relevant stems in/out
Transitions between states by tweening stem volumes (fade in combat drums, fade out ambient melody) rather than abruptly cutting or crossfading between two separate non-synchronized tracks

Does NOT implement adaptive music as simply calling stop() on one AudioStreamPlayer and play() on a different one — this causes an audible silence gap and the new track starts from the beginning rather than the correct beat

evals.name: sprite-hit-flash-outline
evals.prompt: I'm making a 2D game in Godot 4. I need two visual effects: (1) a white flash on my sprites when they take damage, so players can clearly see a hit registered, and (2) a colored outline/glow around interactable objects so players know they can interact with them. How do I write these shaders in Godot?

assertions.text: Both effects use shader_type canvas_item (not spatial or sky) — 2D sprite effects require the canvas_item shader type in Godot

Hit flash: the fragment shader replaces the visible pixel color with white (or a mix toward white) while preserving the original texture's alpha — so only non-transparent pixels flash, not the whole bounding box

Hit flash is controlled by a shader uniform (e.g. flash_amount: float 0.0–1.0 or flash_active: bool) set from GDScript via set_shader_parameter(), then reset after a short duration via a tween or timer

Outline: samples the texture at offset UV positions in N/S/E/W (or 8) directions; where the current pixel is transparent but an adjacent sample is opaque, renders the outline color — this is the UV-offset expansion approach, not a post-process on the whole screen
Outline color and size are exposed as shader uniforms so they're tunable from the Inspector without editing the shader source
Does NOT recommend a post-process effect applied to the entire screen for per-sprite hit flash or outline — these are per-sprite ShaderMaterial effects

evals.name: dissolve-shader
evals.prompt: I want a dissolve effect for when enemies die in my 2D game in Godot 4 — the sprite should disintegrate over about half a second, starting from random-looking parts of the sprite rather than fading out uniformly. How do I make this?

assertions.text: Uses a noise texture (NoiseTexture2D resource) sampled in the fragment shader to determine which pixels dissolve first — pixels with noise value below a threshold disappear, producing a non-uniform, organic dissolution pattern
The dissolve threshold is a shader uniform (e.g. dissolve_amount: float, 0.0 = fully visible → 1.0 = fully dissolved) that is animated from GDScript via a tween on the shader parameter

Uses 'discard' in the fragment function to remove dissolved pixels — NOT setting the alpha channel to 0.0, because discarding is required for correct rendering order with other transparent objects in Godot's canvas_item pipeline

Optionally adds an edge effect: pixels near the dissolve threshold boundary receive a bright or emissive color (e.g. orange/fire glow) so the dissolve has a burning/energized edge rather than just a hard cutoff
The dissolve animation is driven from GDScript as a Tween on the shader parameter, with queue_free() called when the tween completes — NOT a separate animated texture or sprite-sheet approach

evals.name: multiplayer-scope-trap
evals.prompt: I'm making a 2D co-op action RPG in Godot 4. My solo game is done and plays great. Should I add online multiplayer? How hard is it really, and what approach should I take?

assertions.text: Leads with an honest scope warning: adding online multiplayer to a finished solo game typically adds 30–100%+ more development time — it is NOT a 'just sync the state' addition, even for a finished game

Clearly distinguishes local co-op (same machine, shared input, nearly trivial to add) from online multiplayer (latency, packet loss, desync, game state synchronization — fundamentally different problems requiring architectural changes)
Recommends starting with local co-op / split-screen as the first step toward co-op — ship that, then evaluate online — rather than jumping straight to online networking

If online is pursued: recommends an authoritative server architecture (one machine owns the true game state; clients send inputs and receive updates) rather than naive peer-to-peer state sync, which is vulnerable to cheating and desync

Names Godot's built-in MultiplayerAPI and at least one relay/backend service or third-party library (Nakama, Photon, or similar) — explains that direct P2P connections usually require a relay server for NAT traversal

Does NOT say 'just sync position and health' as if networking is a simple add-on — acknowledges latency, cheating prevention, disconnect/reconnect handling, and desync as real problems requiring real design

evals.name: rollback-netcode
evals.prompt: I'm building a 2D fighting game in Godot 4. Everyone says rollback netcode is the gold standard for fighting games. What is it, how does it work, and should I implement it myself?

assertions.text: Correctly explains rollback: each client predicts the opponent's input (typically last known), simulates forward, and when the true input arrives, rolls back the game state to the divergence frame and re-simulates forward from there — corrections are invisible if latency is low

Distinguishes rollback from delay-based netcode: delay-based adds input delay so both clients always have each other's inputs before simulating (simpler, but feels bad at variable latency); rollback hides latency through speculation and correction, feeling much better in practice

States the hard requirement: the game simulation must be fully deterministic — same inputs always produce exactly the same outputs, with seeded RNG, no random behavior outside of seeded generators, and no floating-point platform divergence
Names GGPO or the Godot Rollback Netcode addon (by Snopek / GDRollback) as the existing library to use — strongly recommends against implementing rollback from scratch, which is expert-level work

Scopes rollback to where it is appropriate: low-player-count, fast-paced, latency-sensitive games (fighting games, beat-em-ups, some RTS) — NOT for MMOs, large-world games, or games with many synchronized objects
Does NOT recommend rollback as the universal correct choice for all multiplayer games — it is the right choice specifically for fighting games; other game types have better-suited approaches

evals.name: roguelike-run-save
evals.prompt: I'm making a roguelike in Godot 4. I need players to be able to save mid-run and quit, then resume later — but death must be permanent and players start over from scratch. I also want meta-progression: permanent upgrades that persist between runs (like unlocked characters and bonus starting items). How do I structure this?

assertions.text: Separates two distinct save files: a run save (volatile — deleted on death or run completion) and a meta save (permanent — persists across all runs, tracks unlocks, currency, best stats)
The run save serializes logical game state — floor number, inventory as item IDs + quantities, current stats, dungeon seed, explored flags — NOT engine objects, scene trees, or node hierarchies
Includes a version field in the save file from day one, so future content additions can migrate existing saves rather than breaking them

Describes the run lifecycle: on game start check for an existing run save → prompt to resume or start new. On death: delete the run save, tally results into the meta save. On run completion: same meta-update then delete run save.
The meta save is minimal and persistent: unlocked characters/items, earned permanent currency, best-run records — NOT a snapshot of the current run state
Does NOT recommend saving the entire scene tree, node hierarchy, or engine objects — only the logical data model that can be used to reconstruct the game state from scratch

evals.name: save-format-versioning
evals.prompt: I've shipped my roguelike and players have save files from v1.0. In my next update I'm adding a new 'Stamina' stat and reorganizing how items are stored in the save file. How do I update my save format without corrupting or discarding everyone's existing saves?

assertions.text: Centers the solution on a version field in the save file — every save file has an integer version number, and the load function checks it to determine what migrations to run

Implements a migration chain: load the file, read version, run migrations in order (migrate_v1_to_v2, migrate_v2_to_v3, etc.) until reaching the current version — each migration transforms the old structure to the new one
For the new Stamina stat: the migration sets a sensible default value (not null, not 0 if 0 would be unplayable) for any save that doesn't have it yet
For the reorganized item storage: the migration reads the old item format and writes the new format field-by-field — it does not simply discard or ignore items that don't match the new schema
Recommends backing up the original save file before writing the migrated version (copy to a .bak file), so players can recover if migration has a bug

Does NOT recommend deleting old saves or requiring players to start over as the primary solution, and does NOT recommend checking for field presence (hasattr / has()) as a substitute for proper versioned migrations — that approach becomes unmaintainable after multiple updates

evals.name: signal-driven-hud
evals.prompt:
My Godot platformer has a player that loses HP when hit. In my player script I wrote:

```gdscript
func take_damage(amount):
    hp -= amount
    get_node("/root/HUD/HealthBar").value = hp
```

Is this the right approach? How should I structure the HUD update?

assertions.text: Identifies the direct node reference as tightly coupled and explains why it's a problem (HUD path changes break it; player knows about UI implementation)
Recommends emitting a signal from the player (e.g. health_changed) instead of calling into the HUD directly
Shows the HUD connecting to the player signal and updating the bar in response — NOT the player calling any HUD method
Recommends tweening the health bar value (e.g. Tween.tween_property) rather than setting it instantly — instant snaps look cheap and mask hits
Places the HUD in a CanvasLayer so it is immune to camera movement and zoom
Does NOT recommend using get_node with a hardcoded absolute path (/root/HUD/...) as the solution — that is the antipattern being fixed

evals.name: scene-transition-typewriter
evals.prompt: In my Godot RPG: (1) When I change scenes it cuts instantly — how do I add a fade-to-black transition? (2) My NPC dialogue appears all at once — how do I add a typewriter effect that reveals text character by character, with the player able to skip it?

assertions.text: Scene transition uses a CanvasLayer autoload (or equivalent high-layer node) with a ColorRect overlay that tweens alpha 0→1 before changing scene, then 1→0 after
The fade CanvasLayer has a high layer number (e.g. 128) so it renders above all game content
Typewriter effect uses a Timer node that fires repeatedly, appending one character to the label's text per tick — NOT a sleep loop or await chain for each character
Uses RichTextLabel instead of Label to support BBCode formatting (bold, color, wave animation) in dialogue
Punctuation characters (period, comma, exclamation) cause a longer pause than regular characters during typewriter reveal
Skip input (e.g. ui_accept press while typing) immediately shows the full text rather than waiting for the timer to finish all characters

evals.name: wall-jump-slide
evals.prompt: I'm making a metroidvania in Godot 4. My CharacterBody2D can jump and move left/right. How do I add wall sliding (slower fall when pressing into a wall) and wall jumping (jump away from the wall)?

assertions.text: Wall slide uses a reduced gravity constant (not the normal fall gravity) applied when the player is on a wall AND pressing toward it AND falling (velocity.y > 0)
Uses get_wall_normal() to determine which direction to jump — the wall jump horizontal velocity is wall_normal.x * some speed, NOT a hardcoded direction
Saves the wall normal while touching the wall so it's available after the player leaves the wall surface (wall_cling_timer grace window, mirroring coyote time logic)
Wall jump sets velocity directly (velocity.x = ...; velocity.y = ...) rather than using apply_force or add_force — forces fight the controller and feel sludgy
Uses is_on_wall_only() (not is_on_wall()) to avoid triggering wall jump when the player is standing on a floor that also has a wall component
Does NOT use apply_force, apply_impulse, or RigidBody2D physics for the wall jump — the character is a CharacterBody2D with direct velocity control

evals.name: moving-platform-one-way
evals.prompt: My Godot 4 platformer needs two things: (1) One-way platforms the player can jump up through and drop down through (by pressing down+jump). (2) A moving platform that carries the player without the player sliding off.

assertions.text: One-way platforms use CollisionShape2D with one_way_collision = true on the platform body (not a custom collision mask hack or area sensor)

Drop-through mechanic temporarily disables the player's collision mask for the platform layer (e.g. set_collision_mask_value) for a short duration (~0.15–0.2s) rather than disabling the platform itself
Moving platform uses AnimatableBody2D (not StaticBody2D or RigidBody2D) — StaticBody2D does not report platform velocity, which breaks get_platform_velocity()
Player code calls get_platform_velocity() and adds it to velocity when is_on_floor() is true — this is what makes the player ride with the platform instead of sliding off
Moving platform uses move_and_collide() (not move_and_slide or position assignment) so it physically pushes the CharacterBody2D player rather than passing through
Does NOT recommend parenting the player to the platform as the solution — this causes coordinate-space issues and breaks when the player jumps off

evals.name: branching-dialogue-data
evals.prompt: I'm building an RPG in Godot with lots of NPC dialogue. Some conversations have choices that branch the story, and some lines should only appear if the player has done something (e.g. already talked to another NPC). How should I structure the dialogue data? I want it to be easy to edit and expandable.

assertions.text: Recommends a data-driven approach — dialogue lives in Resource files, JSON, or an external tool (Dialogic/Ink), NOT hardcoded as strings or arrays in GDScript
Each dialogue line has an id, speaker, text, and a next_id reference (not an index integer) — navigating by named id rather than array index makes the graph maintainable as it grows
Choice branches each have their own next_id pointing to the target line — the branching is expressed as data (which id to jump to), not as code (if/elif blocks)

Conditions on lines or choices are stored as a string expression evaluated at runtime (e.g. via Godot's Expression class or an equivalent) against a central game-state object — NOT as boolean variables queried in the dialogue runner code
Recommends or mentions Dialogic 2 or Ink (with godot-ink) as suitable tools for complex branching — does not recommend rolling a custom system unless the game's needs are simple
Does NOT recommend a flat string array with index arithmetic (e.g. dialogue[0], dialogue[1]) as the branching mechanism — that becomes unmaintainable past 3 choices

evals.name: hitscan-vs-projectile
evals.prompt: I'm making a top-down shooter in Godot. I have two weapon types: a sniper rifle that should hit instantly at long range, and a slow rocket that players can dodge. Should I implement these differently? I was going to just spawn a bullet scene for both.

assertions.text: Correctly identifies that the sniper rifle should use hitscan (a raycast that resolves immediately the same frame) — spawning a fast projectile scene for instant-feel weapons is wasteful and can miss targets between frames
Correctly identifies that the rocket should use a spawned projectile node (moves over time, can be dodged, has travel time) — hitscan would remove all dodge opportunity
Shows hitscan using PhysicsRayQueryParameters2D (or 3D equivalent) and direct_space_state.intersect_ray() — NOT a moving invisible bullet node at extreme speed
Warns that spawning bullet scenes for high fire-rate weapons (machine guns, etc.) is expensive and recommends either hitscan or a bullet pool for those cases
Bullet pool or object pool is mentioned for any spawned projectile to avoid per-shot instantiation cost
Does NOT recommend spawning a projectile scene at extreme speed as the hitscan solution — an invisible fast-moving node can miss collision between frames at high speed

evals.name: weapon-firing-modes
evals.prompt: I want to implement a weapon system in Godot with three firing modes: semi-auto (one shot per trigger press), burst (3 shots then cooldown), and full-auto (hold to fire). There's also a reload mechanic. How should I structure this?

assertions.text: Uses an enum state machine with states like IDLE, FIRING, RELOADING (and optionally EMPTY) — NOT nested if/elif blocks checking multiple boolean flags simultaneously
Each state has its own tick function or match branch that handles input and transitions — input checking is inside the state, not in a flat _process function
Semi-auto uses is_action_just_pressed (not is_action_pressed) so each trigger pull fires exactly one shot regardless of how long held
Full-auto uses is_action_pressed and a fire_timer cooldown between shots based on fire_rate (rounds per second)
Weapon configuration (magazine_size, fire_rate, reload_time, burst_count) lives in a WeaponData Resource (or ScriptableObject equivalent) — NOT hardcoded in the weapon script
Burst mode tracks a burst_count variable and transitions back to IDLE after firing the specified number of shots, not after a time delay

evals.name: boss-phase-fsm
evals.prompt: I'm designing a boss fight in Godot with 3 phases. Phase 1 (full HP): slow attacks. Phase 2 (below 60% HP): adds a new fast attack. Phase 3 (below 25% HP): becomes enraged, arena changes. How do I structure this cleanly? My current code is getting messy with nested if statements.

assertions.text: Uses a phase Resource (or equivalent data class) with a health_threshold field — phase transitions trigger when HP drops below the threshold, not checked inline in attack logic
Attack patterns are stored as data (Array of AttackData resources or equivalent) attached to each phase — the boss controller reads available attacks from the current phase, not from hardcoded lists
Attack selection uses weighted random (or at minimum random choice from available attacks with distance/cooldown filtering) — NOT always the same attack in sequence
Every attack has a telegraph phase before it becomes active: a windup animation or warning indicator fires for 0.5–1.5 seconds before the hitbox or damage is activated
Phase transitions emit signals or call methods to trigger arena changes (spawn hazards, change music stem) — the controller separates phase-transition effects from attack logic
Boss is invincible (or has damage mitigation) during its own attack animation active frames — players cannot trivially spam damage during the boss's own attacks

evals.name: camera-room-zones
evals.prompt: I'm making a 2D metroidvania in Godot. I want the camera to be locked to each room — when the player walks through a door, the camera smoothly transitions to show the new room rather than following the player freely. How do I implement this?

assertions.text: Uses Area2D nodes (one per room) that detect when the player enters and trigger a camera bound update
Sets Camera2D limit_left, limit_right, limit_top, limit_bottom to the room's bounds — the built-in limit system automatically clamps the camera to the room without extra math
Smoothly tweens the camera limits (or the camera position) rather than hard-setting them instantly — instant cuts feel like a glitch
Room bounds are derived from the Area2D's CollisionShape2D size/position — NOT hardcoded pixel coordinates for each room
Does NOT recommend disabling Camera2D smoothing and manually setting global_position every frame as the primary room-lock approach — limit_* is the correct tool
Does NOT recommend parenting the Camera2D to the room node as a way to lock it — that would require re-parenting on every room change and loses smooth following

evals.name: cone-of-vision-stealth
evals.prompt: I'm building a stealth game in Godot. Guards should detect the player if the player is within a 90-degree cone in front of the guard AND has line of sight (no walls in between). Detection should not be instant — it should fill up over time. How do I implement this?

assertions.text: Detection pipeline runs cheapest check first: (1) distance check, (2) angle/FOV check using dot product against the guard's facing direction, (3) raycast for line of sight — raycast only fires if both distance and angle pass
FOV check uses dot product (to_player.normalized().dot(facing_direction) > cos(half_fov_radians)) — NOT atan2 or angle() which are slower and less readable for this purpose
Detection is gradual: a detection_level float increases over time while the player is in the cone (e.g. +=  detection_rate * delta) and decreases when out of sight — NOT a single boolean is_seen
State machine has at least PATROL, SUSPICIOUS, and ALERT states — SUSPICIOUS triggers when detection_level crosses a low threshold, ALERT when it reaches 1.0
The raycast uses a specific collision mask that only hits walls/obstacles — NOT all physics bodies, which would make the guard unable to see through other guards or items
Does NOT check every frame with an unconditional raycast from guard to player — the distance and angle pre-checks are essential before the expensive raycast

evals.name: alert-state-machine
evals.prompt: My stealth game guard currently just has is_alerted: bool. When alerted the guard chases the player; when not alerted it patrols waypoints. I need the guard to also have a 'suspicious' state (heard a noise, moves to investigate) and a 'searching' state (lost sight of player, searches the area). How do I restructure this?

assertions.text: Replaces the boolean flag with an enum or string state variable with at least PATROL, SUSPICIOUS, ALERT, and SEARCH states

Uses a state machine pattern: each state has its own tick function (or match branch), and transitions happen through a dedicated _enter_state or _transition method — NOT scattered if/elif checks throughout _physics_process
SUSPICIOUS state moves the guard toward the last known position or sound source, plays a look-around animation, and transitions to ALERT if the player is spotted or SEARCH if suspicion fades
SEARCH state generates a set of search positions around the last known player position and visits them — NOT a timer that simply waits and returns immediately to PATROL
Guards return to the nearest waypoint when resuming PATROL — NOT always restarting from waypoint index 0, which would be an obvious tell players could exploit
last_known_position is stored per-guard (not a global variable) so different guards can have different last known positions and search independently

evals.name: minimap-implementation
evals.prompt: I'm building a top-down RPG in Godot and want to add a minimap in the corner of the screen showing the player's position and nearby enemies. What's the best approach?

assertions.text: Presents two approaches: (1) SubViewport with a separate zoomed-out Camera2D that shares the main World2D — shows everything automatically; (2) icon overlay that manually computes entity positions relative to the player — simpler but requires explicit tracking of each entity type
For the SubViewport approach: explicitly states that the SubViewport must share the same World2D as the main viewport so that the same nodes appear in both renders
Minimap is displayed in a CanvasLayer in the HUD — NOT placed in the game world, which would make it move with the camera

For the icon approach: entity positions are converted to minimap coordinates by computing position relative to player, dividing by a world_radius scale factor, then mapping to the minimap rect — NOT by directly using world coordinates
Mentions using a circular clip mask (via shader or TextureRect with a circular texture mask) to make the minimap round rather than a hard square
Does NOT recommend rendering the minimap by duplicating all game nodes into a separate scene — that would require manual sync and is far more complex than a shared World2D viewport

evals.name: bullet-hell-patterns
evals.prompt: I'm making a bullet hell game in Godot. My boss needs to fire three different attack patterns: (1) a ring of 12 bullets in all directions, (2) a spiral that slowly rotates, (3) bullets aimed directly at the player. I want these to be reusable and composable. How should I structure this?

assertions.text: Bullet pool is mandatory and presented as the first architectural decision — pre-allocates bullets at game start (e.g. 800 bullets) and recycles them instead of instantiate/queue_free per shot
Pattern math uses polar coordinates (angle + direction vector via Vector2.from_angle() or equivalent) — NOT hardcoded x/y offsets, which break when the pattern rotates
Circle pattern evenly distributes bullets using TAU / bullet_count as the angular step between each bullet
Spiral pattern advances a cumulative angle variable each salvo (not each bullet) — the angle accumulates across fire ticks to produce the rotation effect
Pattern configuration lives in a Resource (BulletPatternData or equivalent ScriptableObject) with fields like bullet_count, fire_rate, spread_angle — NOT hardcoded values inside the boss script
PatternEmitter nodes (one per pattern) are separate child nodes of the boss — composing a complex attack means enabling multiple emitters simultaneously, not writing one monolithic fire() function

evals.name: fog-of-war
evals.prompt: I'm making a top-down RPG in Godot and want fog of war: areas the player hasn't visited should be completely black, areas they've visited but can't currently see should be darkened, and the area immediately around the player should be fully visible. How do I implement this?

assertions.text: Uses a grid-based approach where each cell has one of three states: UNSEEN (fully black), REVEALED (darkened — visited but not currently visible), and VISIBLE (fully clear around the player)
Each frame: all currently VISIBLE cells are first set to REVEALED, then cells within the player's vision radius are set to VISIBLE — this produces the correct three-state behavior
The fog grid is stored as a flat array (PackedByteArray or equivalent) indexed by (row * width + col) — NOT a 2D array of Vector2 objects or Dictionary, which are slower and more memory-heavy

Fog is rendered by drawing colored rectangles over each cell in _draw() (using CanvasItem.draw_rect or a TileMap layer) — NOT by placing individual ColorRect nodes for every cell, which would be thousands of nodes
queue_redraw() is called to update the fog visual — and ideally only when the player moves to a new cell, not unconditionally every frame
Mentions that the fog grid should be serialized to the save file (e.g. PackedByteArray.hex_encode()) so exploration progress persists between sessions

evals.name: dialogue-tool-choice
evals.prompt: I'm building a narrative-heavy RPG in Godot with hundreds of lines of dialogue, complex branching, story variables that affect which lines appear, and multiple endings. Should I use Dialogic 2, write my own dialogue system, or use something else?

assertions.text: Recommends Ink (with the godot-ink addon) as the strongest choice for complex branching narrative with variables, conditions, and multiple endings — Ink is designed exactly for this use case
Explains what Ink provides: a dedicated narrative scripting language, knots/stitches for organization, variables and conditions native to the language, compiled to JSON
Positions Dialogic 2 as better suited for cutscene-heavy games with moderate branching and a visual timeline editor workflow — not the best fit for deeply branching narrative
Explicitly advises against hand-rolling a custom dialogue system for hundreds of lines with complex branching — the maintenance burden becomes enormous
Mentions that Ink variables can sync bidirectionally with Godot (reading/writing Ink variables from GDScript) to integrate story state with game systems
Does NOT recommend a flat string array or a simple Resource graph as the primary solution for hundreds of lines with complex branching and multiple endings

evals.name: lock-on-camera
evals.prompt: I'm making a 3D action game in Godot. When the player presses a button, the camera should lock on to the nearest enemy and track both the player and the enemy. The player should be able to cycle through targets. When the enemy dies, lock-on should release.

assertions.text: Target acquisition uses both distance and FOV angle checks — NOT just nearest enemy globally, which could lock onto enemies behind the player
Camera position during lock-on is interpolated toward a point between the player and the target (midpoint or offset toward target) — NOT just looking at the target from the fixed follow position
Checks is_instance_valid(target) each frame to detect if the locked-on enemy has been freed/deleted, and releases lock-on automatically when it has
Target cycling uses the same candidate list sorted by distance — cycling forward increments an index into the sorted array
A UI indicator (sprite or marker) is displayed above the locked-on target — in 3D this requires projecting the 3D world position to 2D screen position
Does NOT recommend using Camera3D.look_at(target.position) directly as the lock-on camera behavior — that produces instant snapping; lerp or tween toward the desired orientation is required

evals.name: boss-telegraph
evals.prompt: Players keep saying my boss attacks feel unfair and 'come out of nowhere.' The boss has 4 attacks and I'm using match state: to handle them. What design patterns should I use to make the attacks feel telegraphed and fair?

assertions.text: Identifies the core problem: attacks have no telegraph phase — there is no windup animation or warning indicator before damage activates, so players have no time to react
Recommends a three-phase structure for every attack: telegraph (warning, 0.5–1.5 seconds), active (damage frames), recovery (boss is vulnerable)
Concrete telegraph implementation: play a windup animation AND show a danger indicator at the impact location (radial warning ring, directional arrow, color change) before damage activates
Boss is invincible or has heavy damage reduction during the telegraph and active frames — vulnerable during recovery — so players must learn patterns rather than just tanking
Recommends extracting each attack into AttackData (or equivalent) with telegraph_duration as a configurable field — NOT a hardcoded await timer buried in a match branch
Does NOT recommend reducing damage or HP as the primary solution to 'feels unfair' — those are band-aids; the real fix is readable attack telegraphing so players can learn and react

evals.name: homing-bullet-pool
evals.prompt: My bullet hell game boss fires 200 bullets at once and my FPS drops to 15. How do I fix this? Also, I want some bullets to slowly home toward the player after being fired.

assertions.text: Identifies instantiate() / queue_free() per bullet as the primary performance culprit — allocating 200 nodes at once triggers GC and node tree overhead
Solution is a pre-allocated bullet pool: instantiate all bullets at game start, hide unused ones, show and init them when fired, return them to the pool when done (hide + disable physics)

Homing is implemented by rotating the bullet's velocity vector toward the player each frame by a maximum turn angle (homing_strength * delta radians) — NOT by setting velocity to (player_pos - bullet_pos).normalized() * speed, which produces instant lock-on
The turn rate cap is explicitly mentioned as the key tuning knob — too high makes the bullet uncatchable; a moderate value gives players a chance to outmaneuver homing bullets
Bullet collision uses Area2D signals (body_entered or area_entered) — NOT a manual distance check loop over all active bullets each frame, which would be O(n) per frame

Does NOT recommend reducing bullet count as the primary performance fix — pooling eliminates the allocation cost so 200 pooled bullets is fine; reducing count is a game design change, not a performance fix

evals.name: behavior-tree-npc-ai
evals.prompt: I have a guard NPC with 12 states in a giant FSM: patrolling, investigating a sound, chasing, searching after losing the player, flanking, calling for backup, retreating when low health, taking cover, healing, returning to patrol, idle variants, and a scripted cutscene state. The transition logic is becoming impossible to maintain — every state needs to check 'am I dead? am I stunned? did I hear something?' How should I restructure this?

assertions.text: Recommends a Behavior Tree over the FSM for this complexity — names state-count explosion and cross-cutting concern checks (dead/stunned/heard) as the specific reasons BTs are a better fit

Explains the three core BT node types: Sequence (all children must succeed in order, short-circuits on first failure), Selector (first child to succeed wins, short-circuits on first success), and Leaf nodes (Action and Condition)
Introduces a Blackboard (shared dictionary of world state: target_position, alert_level, last_heard_position, health_pct) that all nodes read from rather than nodes reaching into each other

Shows a concrete tree structure for the guard — either as pseudocode hierarchy or as GDScript BTNode implementations — demonstrating composability (e.g. a patrol subtree reused across multiple enemy types)
Recommends LimboAI or Beehave as Godot addons, OR provides a hand-rolled GDScript BTNode base class with a tick() method returning a Status enum (SUCCESS/FAILURE/RUNNING)
Names when NOT to use BTs: simple 3-state enemies (FSM is fine), one-off scripted sequences (use AnimationPlayer + signal), or when the overhead of ticking every node every frame exceeds budget

evals.name: selector-vs-sequence
evals.prompt: I'm implementing a behavior tree for my enemies. I keep confusing when to use a Selector node versus a Sequence node. Can you explain the difference and give concrete examples of when I'd use each?

assertions.text: Sequence = AND logic: all children must succeed in order; returns FAILURE immediately when any child fails (short-circuit); analogy: 'do A, then B, then C — if any step fails, the whole plan fails'

Selector = OR logic: returns SUCCESS as soon as any child succeeds (short-circuit); tries each child in priority order as a fallback; analogy: 'try the best option first, fall back to the next if it fails'
Gives a concrete game example for Sequence: AttackSequence = [MoveInRange → FaceTarget → FireWeapon] where all three must succeed in order for the attack to land
Gives a concrete game example for Selector: CombatSelector = [TakeHealingItem (if available), TakeCover (if cover exists), FleeCombat] — tries the best option, falls back if it's not possible
Explains how nesting Sequences inside Selectors (and vice versa) creates complex behavior: a root Selector with [CombatSequence, PatrolSequence, IdleAction] is a complete AI loop

Explains RUNNING status: a node (typically an Action leaf) returns RUNNING when it needs multiple frames to complete (e.g. moving to a position); the tree re-ticks this node on subsequent frames until it returns SUCCESS or FAILURE

evals.name: animationtree-locomotion
evals.prompt: My 3D character has walk, run, and idle animations and a separate jump animation. When I switch between them using animation_player.play() the transitions are instant and jarring — the character pops between poses. How do I set up smooth blending in Godot 4?

assertions.text: Uses AnimationTree (not just AnimationPlayer.play()) as the solution — specifically explains that AnimationTree enables blending between states rather than instant cuts

Uses an AnimationNodeStateMachine inside AnimationTree for state-based animation; shows how to add states (idle, walk, run, jump) and transitions between them with a transition_time/duration so blending is smooth

Uses a BlendSpace1D (or AnimationNodeBlend1D) for the locomotion layer: idle→walk→run blended by a speed float parameter; sets the blend_position parameter from GDScript each frame based on velocity.length()

Shows how to set AnimationTree parameters from GDScript using the correct API: anim_tree.set('parameters/StateMachine/conditions/is_jumping', true) or anim_tree['parameters/BlendSpace1D/blend_position'] = speed

Explains root motion vs in-place animation: root motion extracts movement from the animation clip itself (animator controls position), in-place animations loop at origin (code controls position); recommends in-place for character controllers
Does NOT recommend calling animation_player.play() directly for locomotion — names this as the bug (bypasses AnimationTree blending, causes pops)

evals.name: upper-body-aim-layer
evals.prompt: In my third-person shooter, I want the character's upper body to aim at the target (rotating torso/spine/head) while the lower body plays the normal locomotion animation independently. How do I set up layered animation like this in Godot 4?

assertions.text: Uses AnimationNodeBlendTree (not a simple StateMachine) as the animation tree type — explains that BlendTree enables compositing multiple animation streams together via Add/Blend nodes

Shows the correct setup: a locomotion AnimationNode feeds the lower body; an aim AnimationNode (BlendSpace2D keyed by pitch+yaw, or a procedural rotation) feeds the upper body; an AnimationNodeAdd2 or AnimationNodeBlend2 with a bone mask combines them

Describes the bone mask on the blend node: a mask that includes only upper body bones (spine, chest, neck, arms) so the lower body locomotion passes through unaffected while the upper body plays the aim layer

Covers how to drive the aim layer: either a BlendSpace2D with 8 aim direction animations blended by horizontal and vertical angles, OR SkeletonIK3D / look_at rotation applied to the spine bone procedurally after the animation tree runs

Mentions animation events / call track integration: footstep sounds, shell ejection effects, hit detection enabling/disabling — all triggered via AnimationPlayer call tracks at specific frames, not via timer-based code
Does NOT recommend manually setting bone rotations every frame to face the target without blending — names this as the wrong approach (produces jitter and fights the animation)

evals.name: ik-foot-placement
evals.prompt: My 3D character looks like it's hovering or sinking into slopes because its feet don't adapt to the terrain. The animations look fine on flat ground but terrible on hills and stairs. How do I add procedural foot placement in Godot 4?

assertions.text: Uses SkeletonIK3D (or SkeletonModifier3D in Godot 4.3+) as the IK solver — attaches to the Skeleton3D node, sets root_bone and tip_bone (e.g. 'Hips' → 'LeftFoot'), and sets a target NodePath to a Marker3D that gets repositioned each frame
Uses RayCast3D (or PhysicsRayQueryParameters3D direct cast) shooting downward from each foot bone's current world position to find the terrain surface; the hit point becomes the IK target position
Blends IK weight (SkeletonIK3D.interpolation) rather than toggling start()/stop() — lerps interpolation from 0→1 when on slope/stairs and from 1→0 on flat ground or during jumps/dashes
Adjusts pelvis/hip height based on average foot offset: if both feet are lower than expected, push the body down by half the average offset to prevent legs from stretching unnaturally
Places foot placement updates in _process (visual/cosmetic) NOT _physics_process — explains that IK is a rendering correction, not a physics simulation, and should run at render framerate

Does NOT recommend manually setting bone Transform3D rotations directly in code as the primary approach — names SkeletonIK3D as the correct tool and explains why direct bone manipulation produces unstable/jittery results without an IK solver

evals.name: ik-hand-grab
evals.prompt: I want my 3D character's hand to naturally reach toward and grab a door handle or ladder rung when the player is near it. How do I implement hand IK for interactive objects in Godot 4?

assertions.text: Places a Marker3D (or Position3D) on the interactive object at the exact grab point (door handle position, ladder rung center); this marker is the IK target — the character's hand tracks to it
Uses SkeletonIK3D for the hand bone chain; sets SkeletonIK3D.target_node to the Marker3D on the interactive object when in range; sets SkeletonIK3D.start() to enable

Detects proximity via Area3D on the interactive object: body_entered triggers IK activation, body_exited triggers deactivation; on activation lerps SkeletonIK3D.interpolation from 0→1; on deactivation lerps back to 0
Smoothly blends in/out by lerping SkeletonIK3D.interpolation (0 = animation only, 1 = full IK) rather than calling start()/stop() abruptly — prevents the hand from teleporting

Handles orientation of the hand at the grab point: the Marker3D's rotation defines the expected hand orientation (palm facing the handle); SkeletonIK3D uses target_node's global_transform for both position and orientation of the tip bone

Does NOT recommend updating the IK target by writing directly to Skeleton3D bone transforms every frame without a solver — names SkeletonIK3D as the correct tool and explains that it handles the bone chain math (FABRIK algorithm) automatically

evals.name: lod-performance
evals.prompt: My 3D forest scene has 500 trees and 300 rocks and the FPS drops to 15. The objects are far away but still rendering at full detail. I've already tried reducing draw distance but that makes everything pop in and out. What's the right approach?

assertions.text: Names Level of Detail (LOD) as the correct solution: use high-poly meshes close up, switch to progressively lower-poly versions at distance, rather than hiding objects entirely (which causes pop-in)

Explains Godot 4's GeometryInstance3D LOD: set lod_min_distance and lod_max_distance on MeshInstance3D; create 2-3 LOD meshes (LOD0 full detail, LOD1 ~50% polys, LOD2 ~10% polys, SHADOW_ONLY or billboard for very far); Godot picks the right mesh automatically

Recommends MultiMeshInstance3D for large numbers of identical objects (trees, rocks, grass): renders thousands of instances in a single draw call via GPU instancing; set instance transforms via Transform3DArray; single physics collision shape for the whole forest patch

Mentions VisibilityNotifier3D (or VisibleOnScreenNotifier3D) to pause AI, animations, and _process on objects that are off-screen or behind the camera — reduces CPU cost even when GPU cost is managed by LOD

Recommends disabling shadow casting on LOD1+ meshes (GeometryInstance3D.cast_shadow = SHADOW_CASTING_SETTING_OFF) and reducing DirectionalLight3D shadow distance — shadows are often the largest GPU cost for many-object scenes

Does NOT recommend reducing draw distance as the primary fix — names it as the wrong tool (causes jarring pop-in) and instead recommends LOD + MultiMesh as the solutions that eliminate the perceptible transition

evals.name: chunk-world-loading
evals.prompt: I'm building an open-world RPG in Godot 4. If I put everything in one scene it'll be huge and take forever to load. How should I structure the world so not everything needs to be in memory at once?

assertions.text: Introduces a chunk grid system: divide the world into fixed-size chunks (e.g. 64×64 or 128×128 world units); track the player's current chunk_coord = floor(player_position / chunk_size); load chunks within load_radius, unload beyond unload_radius (with hysteresis — unload_radius slightly larger to prevent flicker)

Uses ResourceLoader.load_threaded_request(path) for async background loading — NOT load() which blocks the main thread; polls with load_threaded_get_status() in _process; retrieves with load_threaded_get() when status is THREAD_LOAD_LOADED
Maintains a priority queue (sorted by distance to player) so the closest unloaded chunks load first; limits in-flight loading requests to 2-3 at a time to avoid memory spikes

Describes the ChunkManager autoload: stores active_chunks: Dictionary[Vector2i, Node]; on player chunk change, queues new chunks to load and marks distant chunks for unloading (deferred removal via call_deferred('queue_free') to avoid physics teardown mid-frame)

Addresses entity persistence: when a chunk unloads, serialize all dynamic entity states (NPC positions, item states, door open/closed) to a Dictionary in memory (or disk for permanent changes); restore when the chunk reloads
Does NOT recommend putting all world content in a single packed scene or loading all scenes at startup — names both as wrong approaches and explains why (memory, load time, frame hitches)

evals.name: noise-biome-terrain
evals.prompt: I want to procedurally generate a 3D terrain in Godot 4 with different biomes — desert, forest, snowy mountains — based on the terrain height and some other factor. How do I approach this?

assertions.text: Uses FastNoiseLite (Godot 4's built-in noise class) to generate height values: sets noise_type (SimplexSmooth recommended), octaves, frequency, and calls get_noise_2d(x, z) at each grid point to get a height [-1, 1] mapped to a world height range

Uses TWO separate noise maps for biome determination — one for elevation/height and one for moisture/humidity — and defines biomes as a function of both axes: high elevation → snow, low elevation + high moisture → swamp/forest, low moisture → desert

Builds the terrain mesh using SurfaceTool (or ArrayMesh directly): iterates a grid of vertices, adds positions, normals (computed from height differences via cross product of adjacent vertices), and UV coordinates; calls commit() to get a Mesh resource; assigns to MeshInstance3D

Implements texture splatting: encodes biome blend weights as vertex colors or a splatmap texture; uses a ShaderMaterial with 3-4 texture samplers (grass, rock, sand, snow) blended by the weights — NOT switching between Materials per biome
Uses a deterministic seed: FastNoiseLite.seed is set to world_seed (or a hash of chunk coordinates for chunk-based generation) so the same world regenerates identically on reload

Mentions domain warping as an optional improvement: sampling noise at offset coordinates (x + noise2(x,z), z + noise2(z,x)) to produce more organic-looking coastlines and terrain shapes rather than smooth blobs

evals.name: wave-function-collapse
evals.prompt: My procedurally generated tile-based dungeon rooms all look the same — just rectangular rooms connected by corridors. I've heard about Wave Function Collapse for generating more interesting layouts. How does it work and how do I implement it?

assertions.text: Explains the WFC core concept correctly: each cell starts with all possible tile types as valid options; the algorithm collapses cells one at a time (starting with the lowest entropy / fewest options) by randomly picking from remaining options; propagates constraints to neighbors (adjacency rules) to eliminate impossible tiles; repeats until all cells collapsed or a contradiction is reached

Explains adjacency rules: for each tile type, defines which tile types are valid in each direction (left, right, up, down); e.g. a wall tile can be adjacent to floor tiles but not water tiles; these rules are the soul of WFC — they determine what the output looks like

Describes backtracking: when a contradiction occurs (a cell has zero remaining options), the algorithm backtracks to a previous state and tries a different choice; most WFC implementations keep a stack of states or restart from scratch on contradiction

Provides a concrete GDScript implementation sketch: a grid of option_sets (Array[Array[StringName]] or similar), a propagate() function that removes invalid options from neighbors after a collapse, a collapse_one() that picks the min-entropy cell and removes all but one option

Distinguishes WFC from BSP dungeon generation: BSP produces predictable rectangular partitions (fast, simple, boxy); WFC produces varied tile-accurate layouts that respect visual adjacency rules (slower, more complex, more organic-looking)
Addresses performance: WFC for a 50×50 room is fast (< 1ms); for a 200×200 map it can be slow; suggests generating in chunks, or pre-generating during a loading screen on a Thread

evals.name: combo-input-buffer
evals.prompt: My action game has a 3-hit combo: light attack, light attack, heavy finish. Players complain the window to chain hits is either too strict (they miss the combo) or too loose (the heavy fires when they didn't want it). I'm currently using a boolean that stays true for 0.3 seconds. What's the right way to implement this?

assertions.text: Identifies the boolean flag as the wrong tool: it triggers for any press while true (holds continuous input, can't distinguish tap timing) and doesn't remember inputs pressed slightly before the window opens

Implements an input buffer: a short array (ring buffer) of (action_name, timestamp) pairs; appends on Input.is_action_just_pressed(); buffer window is ~0.12 seconds; consumed entries are removed; check buffer against expected_next_input each frame during the combo window

Implements a combo state machine: states are [IDLE, LIGHT_1, LIGHT_2, HEAVY_FINISH]; each step has an expected_next_input and a window_timer; transitioning to the next step requires a buffered matching input within the window; if window expires with no matching input, return to IDLE

Uses ComboStepData Resource (or equivalent data structure) with: animation name, damage, hitbox_active_start, hitbox_active_end, cancel_window_start, cancel_window_end as normalized floats of animation length — data-driven, not hardcoded per-ability

Enables and disables the hitbox via an AnimationPlayer call track (a method call track at the hitbox_active_start/end frames) rather than a parallel timer — prevents phantom hits during recovery frames
Exposes the window duration as an @export float — names this as critical for playtesting because combo timing feel is highly sensitive and will be tuned dozens of times

evals.name: attack-cancel
evals.prompt: I want skilled players to be able to cancel a sword slash mid-animation into a dodge roll. Right now if I press dodge during an attack, nothing happens until the attack finishes. How do I implement attack cancels?

assertions.text: Defines the cancel window as a time range within the attack animation — opened at a specific frame (e.g. 40% through the animation) and closed at another (e.g. 75%); outside this window, dodge input is ignored during the attack; inside it, dodge immediately interrupts the attack

Opens and closes the cancel window via AnimationPlayer call tracks (method call tracks that call enable_cancel_window() and disable_cancel_window() at the appropriate animation frames) — NOT via a parallel Timer node

Buffers the dodge input during the attack (even outside the cancel window) so inputs pressed slightly early are honored when the window opens: checks the input buffer when the cancel window opens, not just at the exact moment of the keypress
On cancel: immediately plays the dodge animation (interrupt attack animation), applies dodge velocity/invincibility frames, resets the combo state machine to IDLE
Establishes input priority: dodge/block cancel > combo continuation > new attack; checks this priority order when consuming buffered inputs during the cancel window

Does NOT recommend allowing cancel on every frame of the attack animation — explains that restricting to a mid-animation window is intentional game design: it rewards players who learn the timing while preventing mashing from bypassing all attack commitment

evals.name: open-world-chunk-design
evals.prompt: I'm making an open world RPG in Godot 4. The world is 4km × 4km with villages, forests, dungeons, and NPCs. If I put everything in one big scene it takes 45 seconds to load and uses 4GB of RAM. How should I restructure this?

assertions.text: Introduces a chunk-based world: divides the 4km×4km map into a grid of fixed-size chunks (e.g. 128m×128m = ~1000 chunks); each chunk is a separate PackedScene stored as its own .tscn file; only chunks within the player's load radius are in memory

Describes entity interest management: NPCs and enemies outside simulation_radius (e.g. 3 chunks) are 'hibernated' — their node is removed from the scene tree but their state (position, health, inventory, schedule) is saved in a Dictionary; restored when the chunk reloads

Addresses world coordinate float precision: recommends origin shifting when the player moves beyond 5000 units from origin — shift ALL active scene objects by -player_position and reset player to (0,0,0); explains why (float32 loses sub-unit precision at > ~8192 units, causing physics jitter)

Recommends a global coordinate system: store entity positions as (chunk_coord: Vector2i, local_offset: Vector3) rather than raw world floats — eliminates precision issues entirely for stored data; convert to world float only for rendering

Separates static (baked geometry, nav mesh) from dynamic (NPCs, items, interactive objects) content per chunk: static is a merged MeshInstance3D (one draw call); dynamic objects are individual nodes that can be individually loaded/unloaded

Does NOT recommend loading all scenes at startup or using a single monolithic scene — quantifies the problem (45s load, 4GB RAM) and explains that chunk streaming is the only viable solution for world sizes beyond ~512m×512m

evals.name: float-precision-origin-shift
evals.prompt: In my large open world game, the player character starts jittering and the physics behaves strangely once they travel about 10km from the starting area. The farther they go, the worse it gets. What's causing this and how do I fix it?

assertions.text: Correctly identifies floating-point precision loss as the root cause: 32-bit floats (which Godot uses for Transform3D positions) have ~7 decimal digits of precision; at coordinate 10000, the smallest representable step is ~0.001 units — causing visible jitter in physics and rendering

Explains why it gets worse with distance: precision degrades logarithmically — at 1000 units the error is ~0.0001, at 10000 it's ~0.001, at 100000 it's ~0.01; sub-centimeter jitter becomes centimeter-scale jitter

Names origin shifting as the correct fix: when the player's world position exceeds a threshold (e.g. 5000 units from origin), move ALL active scene objects by -player_position and reset the player to (0, 0, 0); the world appears the same to the player but coordinates stay near-origin

Shows GDScript for a WorldOriginShifter autoload: detects when player position magnitude > SHIFT_THRESHOLD; iterates all active chunk nodes and subtracts the offset from their global_position; emits a world_shifted(offset) signal so other systems can update cached world positions

Covers what needs updating on an origin shift: NavigationServer3D positions, active physics bodies, particle system origins, any cached Vector3 world positions in scripts (those must connect to world_shifted signal)

Does NOT recommend switching to 64-bit float mode as the first suggestion (Godot 4 has a double-precision build option but it's rarely necessary and has performance implications) — names origin shifting as the correct, lightweight, industry-standard solution

evals.name: car-handling-godot
evals.prompt: How do I create a car in Godot 4 with realistic-feeling handling? I want real suspension, proper weight transfer in corners, grip loss at high speed, and a weighty feel — not a box sliding around on the floor.

assertions.text: Uses VehicleBody3D + 4× VehicleWheel3D child nodes as the correct Godot 4 approach — NOT a CharacterBody3D or RigidBody3D with manual velocity math; explains that VehicleBody3D inherits from RigidBody3D and provides real suspension simulation

Configures VehicleWheel3D: use_as_traction (rear wheels drive), use_as_steering (front wheels steer), wheel_radius (match visual mesh), suspension_travel (spring compression range, e.g. 0.15m), suspension_stiffness (spring strength, 20-40 for a car), suspension_damping (~0.3), wheel_friction_slip (grip, 1.0-1.5)
Sets VehicleBody3D.center_of_mass_mode = CUSTOM with a lowered center_of_mass Vector3 (e.g. y = -0.3) to reduce body roll; explains that higher CoM → more roll and flip tendency, lower → more planted

Uses a speed-dependent steering angle: at low speed allow a wider steering angle (more turning); at high speed reduce the max angle (prevents spin-out); implemented as lerp(max_steer_high_speed, max_steer_low_speed, speed_normalized)

Implements an engine torque curve (Curve resource mapping speed ratio → max torque): high torque at low speed (strong acceleration), tapering off at top speed (natural speed limiter); applies to VehicleBody3D.engine_force each frame

Does NOT recommend using CharacterBody3D or a RigidBody3D with manually computed wheel physics — names this as the wrong approach (loses weight transfer, suspension, and friction simulation that VehicleBody3D provides for free)

evals.name: surface-friction-driving
evals.prompt: My car handles identically on ice, dirt, and asphalt. How do I make the surface under the wheels affect grip, handling, and give feedback to the player?

assertions.text: Detects the surface under each wheel using a PhysicsRayQueryParameters3D raycast downward from each VehicleWheel3D contact point; reads the PhysicsBody3D collider's physics material or a custom surface_type metadata property on the hit object

Applies surface friction by setting VehicleWheel3D.wheel_friction_slip dynamically based on surface type: asphalt ~1.5 (high grip), dirt ~0.9 (reduced grip), ice ~0.4 (very low grip), wet ~0.7; call this every physics frame based on what each wheel is touching

Provides player feedback for surface type: visual (dust/dirt particles on dirt wheels, snow spray on snow), audio (tire squeal on asphalt, crunching on gravel — use AudioStreamPlayer3D at each wheel position), haptic/controller rumble on skid

Detects wheel slip / skidding: compare VehicleWheel3D's lateral velocity to its longitudinal velocity; when the ratio exceeds a threshold, start spawning skidmark geometry (ImmediateMesh trail from contact point) and increase audio pitch of tire squeal
