Handles the transition: don't switch friction instantly on surface change — lerp wheel_friction_slip toward the target value over 0.2-0.3 seconds to avoid abrupt grip changes mid-corner

Does NOT recommend applying a simple force multiplier to the whole vehicle or using a global friction override — explains that per-wheel surface detection is required for realistic weight-transfer effects (one wheel on ice, three on asphalt)

evals.name: ability-pipeline
evals.prompt: I'm building a MOBA-style game in Godot 4. Every ability I add needs: a mana cost, a cooldown, a 0.8-second cast time where the player can be interrupted, and an effect when it fires. Right now I'm copy-pasting timer and boolean logic into each ability script and it's becoming a nightmare to maintain. How should I architect this?

assertions.text: Introduces AbilityData as a Resource (@export fields: ability_id: StringName, mana_cost: float, cooldown: float, cast_time: float, interruptible: bool) — all abilities share this schema; the AbilityComponent reads from it, not from hardcoded values per script

AbilityComponent (an attached node, not a global autoload) owns the activation pipeline: try_activate() checks cost → checks cooldown → checks tags (blocked_by) → consumes mana → enters CASTING state → waits cast_time (interruptible) → fires effect → starts cooldown

Implements interrupt(): if current_state == CASTING and ability.interruptible, cancels the cast, refunds the mana cost, resets to IDLE state — and does nothing if the ability is NOT interruptible (the distinction is critical for balance)

Tracks cooldowns in the AbilityComponent (not in AbilityData): a Dictionary[StringName, float] of ability_id → remaining_seconds, decremented in _process — AbilityData is immutable shared data, cooldown state is per-actor runtime data

Emits signals for UI integration: ability_activated(ability), ability_interrupted(ability), ability_ready(ability, cooldown_remaining) — HUD connects to these signals to drive cooldown overlays without polling

Does NOT recommend subclassing per ability with copy-pasted timer variables — names this as the architecture problem (adding a 10th ability requires touching 10 files); the data-driven AbilityData Resource + unified AbilityComponent pipeline is the fix

evals.name: ability-tags-blocking
evals.prompt: In my game, a 'Silence' debuff should prevent casting abilities tagged as 'spell', and a 'Stun' should block all abilities. How do I implement this kind of tag-based ability gating?

assertions.text: AbilityData has two tag arrays: tags (what this ability IS, e.g. ['spell', 'projectile', 'offensive']) and blocked_by (what debuffs prevent it, e.g. ['silence', 'stun']); these are Arrays of StringName for fast comparison

AbilityComponent maintains active_effect_tags: HashSet[StringName] (or a counted Dictionary for stacking debuffs); Silence status effect adds 'silence' to this set on apply, removes it on expire; Stun adds 'stunned'

In try_activate(): before checking cost or cooldown, check if any tag in ability.blocked_by intersects active_effect_tags; if so, return early with BLOCKED result (and optionally emit an ability_blocked signal for UI feedback like a 'silenced' flash)

Shows how status effects add/remove tags: the EffectManager (from rpg-systems reference) calls ability_component.add_effect_tag('silence') on application and remove_effect_tag('silence') on expiry — the AbilityComponent doesn't need to know about specific debuff types

Handles the 'Stun blocks everything' case: Stun's blocked_by entry is checked against a wildcard or Stun adds a 'stunned' tag that all abilities include in their blocked_by array — the wildcard approach: AbilityComponent checks if active_effect_tags.has('stunned') before even checking per-ability blocked_by

Does NOT recommend a boolean-flag approach (is_silenced: bool, is_stunned: bool per actor) — names this as a dead end that requires touching every actor class for each new debuff type; the tag set approach is O(1) lookup and requires zero changes to add new debuff types

evals.name: utility-ai-enemy
evals.prompt: My game enemies always do the same thing in the same order regardless of the situation — they attack when I'm close, run away when low health, and that's it. I want them to dynamically choose between attacking, retreating, calling reinforcements, taking cover, or healing based on what's actually happening. How do I implement this?

assertions.text: Recommends Utility AI as the correct approach for this scenario: score each available action using functions of game state (health, distance, ammo, cover availability, reinforcements available); pick the highest-scoring action each tick; re-evaluate at a fixed interval (every 0.2-0.5 seconds, not every frame)

Shows a concrete scoring example: each score is normalized to [0,1]; HealthScore = hp / max_hp; DistanceScore = 1 - clamp(distance / max_range, 0, 1); AttackScore = DistanceScore * 0.6 + (1 - HealthScore) * 0.2; FleeScore = (1 - HealthScore) * 0.8; HealScore = (1 - HealthScore) if healing_available else 0.0; pick max

Implements an Action base class with score(actor) → float and execute(actor) methods, plus optional can_use(actor) → bool prerequisite check (e.g. CallReinforcements.can_use() returns false if reinforcements are already called or unavailable)

Adds noise to break ties and prevent predictability: add a small random offset (0-0.05) to each score before comparing; this prevents enemies from always making the same choice when scores are close, making behavior feel less mechanical

Explains when to use Utility AI vs FSM vs GOAP: FSM for simple enemies (< 6 clear states, no tradeoffs); Utility AI for enemies that weigh options (attack vs heal vs flee — genuine tradeoffs with continuous scores); GOAP for enemies that need to plan multi-step sequences to achieve a goal

Does NOT recommend a nested if/elif decision tree for this type of multi-factor decision — explains that a hardcoded decision tree can't be tuned (changing one branch affects all others) and breaks down as soon as a new action is added

evals.name: bt-fsm-goap-choice
evals.prompt: I'm building an RTS with complex unit AI. When should I use a finite state machine, when should I use a behavior tree, and when would I need GOAP? I don't want to over-engineer it.

assertions.text: FSM: best for < 6-8 states with clear, explicit transitions; cheap to implement and debug; transitions are first-class (you can see and test every edge); breaks down when state count grows (n² transition complexity) or when cross-cutting concerns (death, stun, interrupt) must be checked from every state

Behavior Tree: best when behavior is hierarchical and has reusable subtrees (patrol subtree shared by Guard, Soldier, Captain); composable — add new behaviors without modifying existing ones; handles cross-cutting concerns naturally via Decorator nodes (Repeat, Inverter, Cooldown at any level)

GOAP: best when the AI needs to plan a sequence of actions to achieve a goal given dynamic world state preconditions (find ammo → take cover → reload → flank); produces emergent behavior; expensive to implement correctly; overkill unless you specifically need multi-step planning

Gives concrete genre examples: tower defense unit AI → FSM (3 states: idle/move/attack); RPG guard → BT (patrol subtree + alert subtree + combat subtree, all reusable); military squad AI → GOAP or Utility AI (dynamic resource management, flanking, suppression, retreat all interleave)

Gives a decision rule: start with FSM; migrate to BT when the FSM's transition graph becomes unreadable or subtrees need to be shared across enemy types; add Utility AI (not GOAP) when actions have continuous trade-off scores; only use GOAP when enemies genuinely need to plan sequences from world state

Does NOT recommend starting with GOAP for simplicity or as a default — calls it out as the most common over-engineering mistake; recommends FSM → BT as the natural progression path with GOAP as a specialized tool only for specific designs

evals.name: colorblind-modes
evals.prompt: A player told me my game is unplayable for them because they have deuteranopia (green colorblindness) and my entire health/enemy system uses red vs green. How do I add proper colorblind support?

assertions.text: Identifies the root cause: the UI relies on color alone to convey information; the fix has two parts — (1) add colorblind simulation/correction modes as a setting, and (2) redesign elements to not rely on color alone (add shape, icon, or text)

Implements a colorblind post-process shader: a CanvasLayer at a high layer with a ColorRect covering the full screen and a ShaderMaterial; the shader applies a 3×3 color correction matrix (different matrices for Protanopia, Deuteranopia, Tritanopia) to transform colors toward what each type perceives distinctly

Names the rule 'never convey information by color alone': health bars should also show a numeric value or icon; enemy faction should use shape (triangle = hostile, circle = neutral) not just color; minimap should use labeled icons not color dots; damage numbers should be colored AND sized

Recommends a dedicated Accessibility section in the settings menu with colorblind mode selector (None / Protanopia / Deuteranopia / Tritanopia) and a preview panel showing how the current screen would appear — players can evaluate without leaving settings

Suggests using blue/orange or purple/yellow as the primary status color pair instead of red/green — both are distinguishable by all three major colorblind types, unlike red/green which is invisible to ~8% of players (mostly male)

Does NOT recommend 'just adding a colorblind mode toggle' without also fixing the underlying design — explains that the mode helps (color correction improves perception) but the real fix is not relying on red/green distinction as the sole information channel

evals.name: subtitle-system
evals.prompt: My game has a lot of voiced NPC dialogue but no subtitle system. A player messaged me saying they're hard of hearing and the game is inaccessible to them. What's the minimum viable subtitle system I should implement?

assertions.text: Implements a SubtitleManager autoload: receives subtitle requests via a show_subtitle(text: String, speaker: String, duration: float) method; displays via a CanvasLayer at a high layer (always on top of gameplay); uses a Label with autowrap and a Panel background

Positions subtitles at the bottom third of the screen (not center, not top) — explains that center covers gameplay, top covers HUD elements, and bottom-third is the standard broadcast position that players expect and can read without covering the action

Makes text size and background opacity configurable in the settings: sub_text_size: int (default 18, options 14/18/24/32) and sub_background_opacity: float (0.0-0.8); saved to user://accessibility.json; applied immediately without restart
Prefixes speaker name: 'Guard: Watch your step!' — so players know who is speaking without relying on audio direction; optionally color the speaker name differently from the dialogue text

Handles timing: subtitle auto-hides after duration seconds; if a new line arrives before the previous one expires, the previous is immediately replaced (not queued — queuing causes subtitles to lag significantly behind audio)

Signal-driven: DialogueManager (or AudioStreamPlayer for voiced lines) emits a subtitle_requested(text, speaker, duration) signal that SubtitleManager connects to — subtitles are NOT hardcoded as text in individual scene nodes

evals.name: godot-localization
evals.prompt: My Godot 4 game is in English only. I want to add Spanish and Japanese translations. How do I set this up properly?

assertions.text: Uses Godot 4's TranslationServer with a CSV translation file: first column is the key (e.g. MAIN_MENU_PLAY), subsequent columns are locale codes (en, es, ja) and their translations; added via Project Settings → Localization → Translations

Uses tr('KEY') in GDScript code and the translate property or @String in Control nodes (not hardcoded literal strings); explains that tr() automatically returns the localized string for the current locale

Addresses Japanese font requirement: the default Godot font doesn't include CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) characters; must add a CJK-compatible font (e.g. Noto Sans JP) to the Theme's font fallbacks, or as a separate DynamicFont with the CJK font; test with actual Japanese text

Uses format strings instead of string concatenation for translated text containing variables: tr('DAMAGE_DEALT').format({'amount': 42}) NOT 'Dealt ' + str(42) + ' damage' — word order differs between languages and concatenation breaks in non-English

Sets locale at runtime via TranslationServer.set_locale('es') and saves the choice to user://settings.json; Control nodes with the translate property auto-update; custom classes must reconnect to any locale_changed signal and refresh their text

Warns about string overflow: German and Russian translations are 30-60% longer than English; all UI containers must use auto-sizing (not fixed width); test with pseudolocalization (expand all strings by 30% and add accented characters) before getting real translations

evals.name: string-overflow-i18n
evals.prompt: My German and Russian translations are much longer than the English originals and they're overflowing my UI buttons, labels, and text boxes. Some buttons are clipping the text entirely. How do I fix this systematically?

assertions.text: Identifies the root cause: fixed-size UI elements designed for English text length; German averages 30-40% longer, Russian 20-35% longer; the fix is structural — containers must auto-size, not have hardcoded dimensions

Removes fixed minimum_size from Label and Button nodes; uses HBoxContainer/VBoxContainer with size_flags = FILL + EXPAND so containers stretch to accommodate content; buttons auto-width to fit their text instead of having a hardcoded pixel width
Enables Label.autowrap_mode = TextServer.AUTOWRAP_WORD_SMART for multi-line text areas: long strings wrap instead of clipping; pair with a ScrollContainer if the available height is also limited

Tests all locales using pseudolocalization before getting real translations: replace all translation strings with versions padded to 140% of English length with accented characters (e.g. 'Play Game' → 'Þlàÿ Gàmé XXXXXXX'); catches overflow systematically without waiting for translators

Provides a font size scaling option per locale as a last resort: if certain locales genuinely can't fit in the available space even with auto-sizing, allow setting a locale_font_scale in settings (e.g. 0.85 for Russian) to reduce the font size for that locale only

Does NOT recommend truncating translated text with '...' as the primary fix — names this as a last resort that hides information from players and signals poor i18n design; auto-sizing containers are the correct first fix

evals.name: gameplay-telemetry
evals.prompt: I want to add gameplay telemetry to my game so I can see where players are dying, how long levels take to complete, and what paths players are taking through levels. How should I set this up?

assertions.text: Uses event-driven telemetry: discrete events emitted when specific things happen (player_died, level_completed, ability_used) rather than constant state sampling every frame; each event includes event_name, unix_timestamp, session_id, level_id, and a payload Dictionary

Implements a TelemetryManager autoload: session_id is generated at game start (UUID or random large integer, NOT tied to player account); events are appended to an in-memory array and periodically flushed to user://telemetry/{session_id}.json as line-delimited JSON (one JSON object per line, append mode)

Defines the minimum useful event set: session_started (platform, build_version), level_started (level_id, attempt_number), player_died (level_id, position: Vector2/3, cause: String, time_alive_seconds), level_completed (level_id, time_seconds, death_count), session_ended (total_playtime, levels_completed)

Implements death heatmap: store death positions in an Array[Vector2] (or Vector3 for 3D) per level; in a debug/dev build, draw the heatmap as circles overlaid on the level using draw_circle() in a debug CanvasLayer with color scaled by local death density

Records player paths: sample player position every 3-5 seconds (NOT every frame — too much data); store as Array[Vector2] per level segment; visualize as a polyline in the debug overlay to see common routes and exploration gaps

Strips telemetry from release builds or gates it behind a TELEMETRY_ENABLED constant or OS.is_debug_build() check — explains that telemetry must never block gameplay waiting for disk/network I/O and must not exist in production without explicit player consent

evals.name: playtest-instrumentation
evals.prompt: I'm running my first external playtest session next week with 8 players. What's the minimum instrumentation I should build into the game beforehand to get useful data out of the session?

assertions.text: Auto-generates a session log file per playtest run: written to user://playtest_logs/{session_id}.json at game start; includes build_version, timestamp, platform, display_resolution, starting settings; each level attempt appended with start_time, end_time, death_count, completion status

Adds a screenshot shortcut (F9 or a dedicated key) that saves a timestamped PNG to user://screenshots/; includes position and level_id in the filename so testers can take screenshots when they encounter something interesting without stopping to type notes

Adds an in-game feedback button (always visible as a small overlay): opens a simple one-field text input for the tester to type a note; stores the note with current position, current level, and timestamp in the session log — captures observations in-context without interrupting flow

Displays build version string in a corner of the screen (a small Label in a CanvasLayer): version number + date + branch name; critical for correlating feedback to a specific build when running multiple sessions over days or weeks

Anonymizes all data: session_id is a random token (not the tester's name or email); positions are relative to the level, not absolute world coords; no PII collected; explains this both as a privacy requirement and as a trust-building measure with testers

Does NOT recommend surveying players mid-session or asking them to fill out a form while playing — explains that interrupting flow breaks the playtest; collect feedback via the in-game button during play and a post-session survey AFTER they finish

evals.name: godot-gi-choice
evals.prompt: I'm adding lighting to my Godot 4 game. What's the difference between LightmapGI, VoxelGI, and SDFGI, and when should I use each one? Also, what's the step most developers miss when setting up LightmapGI?

assertions.text: States LightmapGI bakes indirect lighting to textures (zero runtime cost, static geometry only)
States VoxelGI bakes to a voxel grid and supports dynamic objects without LightmapGIProbe
States SDFGI is real-time GPU ray marching suited for large open worlds at high GPU cost
Identifies LightmapGIProbe node placement as the most-missed step for dynamic objects to receive indirect lighting in LightmapGI scenes
Provides a decision table or clear routing guidance by scene type (indoor vs outdoor vs open world)
States LightmapGI and VoxelGI cannot both be active on the same geometry simultaneously

evals.name: lightmap-baking
evals.prompt: Walk me through setting up LightmapGI in Godot 4 step by step — from scratch to a baked result. My scene has both static walls and a player character that moves around.

assertions.text: Step 1: generate UV2 for all static meshes via Mesh > Lightmap Unwrap in the editor
Step 2: set gi_mode to BAKED on every static MeshInstance3D in the Inspector
Step 3: add a LightmapGI node to the scene root
Step 4: place LightmapGIProbe nodes throughout the scene for dynamic objects (player) to receive indirect lighting — placement every 4-6m at head height
Step 5: set DirectionalLight/OmniLight bake mode to Static or Dynamic in the Inspector
Step 6: bake via the Lightmap > Bake Lightmaps menu in the editor
Explains that flat/dark dynamic objects (the player) are caused by missing LightmapGIProbe nodes
Mentions UV2 lightmap bleeding from overlapping UV islands as a common baking artifact

evals.name: profiler-workflow
evals.prompt: My Godot 4 game drops below 60fps during combat. How do I diagnose whether this is a CPU or GPU bottleneck, and what's the systematic workflow for finding the specific cause?

assertions.text: Distinguishes GPU-bound from CPU-bound by comparing Process Time + Physics Time against Frame Time in the Debugger Monitor
Names Debug Draw > Overdraw mode for diagnosing GPU fill-rate (fragment shader) bottlenecks
Explains Profiler flame chart should be sorted by Self time (not Total) to find the true bottleneck function
Identifies per-frame allocation (get_nodes_in_group, Array.filter creating new arrays each frame) as a common CPU cause visible as high Self time
Provides the cache pattern fix for per-frame allocations (cache result in _ready or use NodePath caching)
Mentions MultiMeshInstance3D or VisibilityNotifier3D as draw call reduction strategies

evals.name: draw-call-optimization
evals.prompt: My Godot 4 game has 1,000 rock props scattered around the level and the frame rate is bad. How do I diagnose draw call overhead and what's the right way to render 1,000 identical meshes efficiently?

assertions.text: Tells player to check Debugger > Monitor > Render > Draw Calls to measure the current count before optimizing
Provides draw call budget targets: ≤200 mobile, ≤1000 low-end desktop, ≤5000 high-end desktop
Explains that 1,000 individual MeshInstance3D nodes produce 1,000 draw calls but a single MultiMeshInstance3D produces 1
Provides GDScript code showing how to set up a MultiMeshInstance3D with transform array for the 1,000 rocks
Mentions 2D sprite atlas or CanvasItem batching for 2D draw call reduction
Names VisibilityNotifier3D as a way to stop processing off-screen nodes at the CPU level

evals.name: touch-virtual-joystick
evals.prompt: I'm adding a virtual joystick to my mobile Godot 4 game. The joystick needs to support multiple simultaneous touches (so the player can also tap an attack button), have a dead zone, and feel responsive. How do I implement this?

assertions.text: Uses dynamic origin: the joystick base appears where the finger first touches, not at a fixed screen position
Tracks InputEventScreenDrag using the finger_index from the original InputEventScreenTouch to support multi-touch without cross-zone conflicts
Implements dead zone re-mapping as (magnitude - dead_zone) / (1.0 - dead_zone) — not a hard snap to zero — to prevent lurch at threshold
Clamps the stick displacement to MAX_RADIUS using limit_length() or equivalent vector clamp
Claims a finger_index on touch begin and releases it on touch end to prevent other touch zones from capturing mid-drag
Outputs a normalized (or dead-zone-adjusted) direction Vector2 that the player movement code reads each frame

evals.name: mobile-ui-scaling
evals.prompt: I'm porting my Godot 4 game to mobile. My HUD looks broken on different screen sizes and is cut off by the notch on iPhones. What's the correct setup for adaptive UI scaling and safe area handling?

assertions.text: Sets stretch mode to canvas_items and stretch aspect to expand in Project Settings > Display > Window
Uses anchor presets (full rect, top-left, etc.) on all HUD Control nodes instead of fixed pixel positions
Reads DisplayServer.get_display_safe_area() to get notch/home bar insets
Applies safe area margins to a top-level MarginContainer so all HUD children avoid the notch and home bar
Specifies a minimum touch target size of 44pt/px (or equivalent scaled value) for all interactive buttons
Addresses font scaling via a Theme resource or explicit font size scaling rather than relying on default font sizes

evals.name: animationplayer-cutscene
evals.prompt: I want to create a cutscene in Godot 4 where the camera smoothly moves to frame two NPCs talking, dialogue fires at specific times, and the player camera returns at the end. What's the recommended approach using AnimationPlayer?

assertions.text: Uses AnimationPlayer as the time sequencer with property tracks (camera position/rotation) and call method tracks (dialogue, NPC spawning) on the same timeline
Switches to the cutscene camera using cutscene_cam.make_current() at cutscene start
Returns camera to the player camera using player_camera.make_current() at cutscene end
Uses call method tracks to fire game events (spawn NPC, show dialogue, play audio) at specific timestamps rather than polling in _process
Uses get_tree().paused = true during the cutscene with process_mode = PROCESS_MODE_ALWAYS on the AnimationPlayer and camera nodes
Implements a fade-out/fade-in transition (ColorRect + Tween or AnimationPlayer opacity track) around the camera switch to avoid jarring cuts
Uses await anim_player.animation_finished or a signal connection to detect when the cutscene ends

evals.name: cutscene-skip-system
evals.prompt: How do I implement a skippable cutscene system in Godot 4 that prevents accidental skips, captures all input during the cutscene (so the player can't accidentally click through to gameplay), and guarantees the game is in a valid state whether the cutscene plays fully or gets skipped?

assertions.text: Implements a two-press confirm pattern (IDLE -> PENDING -> CONFIRMED with a time window, e.g., 1.5s) to prevent accidental skips
Uses get_tree().paused = true for gameplay input capture during the cutscene, with PROCESS_MODE_ALWAYS on the skip handler and cutscene nodes
skip() and normal completion (animation_finished) both call the same cleanup function — not separate duplicated logic
Disconnects the animation_finished signal before calling anim_player.stop() in skip() to prevent double-calling the cleanup function
Calls a method equivalent to _fire_end_events() to explicitly restore any game state (AI, HUD, input) that would have been set by call tracks between the skip point and the end of the cutscene
Supports marking individual cutscenes as non-skippable (e.g., a skippable parameter on the play() method)

evals.name: visual-shader-editor
evals.prompt: My team has an artist who wants to create shaders for our Godot 4 game but is not comfortable writing GLSL. Should we use the visual shader editor or code-based ShaderMaterial? What are the tradeoffs, and how do we set it up so the artist can work independently?

assertions.text: States visual shader editor and code shader produce identical bytecode with the same runtime performance — the visual editor is an authoring tool, not a different shader type
Recommends visual shader editor for artists who don't write GLSL, with real-time preview and node-based blending/color operations
Recommends code shader when #ifdef compile-time branching (quality tiers) or #include shared function libraries are needed
Explains set_shader_parameter() works identically for visual and code shaders to modify uniforms at runtime from GDScript
Recommends saving the ShaderMaterial as a .tres resource file (not inline on the MeshInstance) so artist edits propagate across all scenes using the material
Mentions the Expression node as a way to write raw GLSL inline within the visual shader graph for math-heavy operations

evals.name: shader-graph-to-code
evals.prompt: My artist built a shader in Godot 4's visual shader editor. I need to modify it programmatically at runtime and also understand how the visual nodes map to actual GLSL. How do I read the graph as code, and how do I change shader values from GDScript?

assertions.text: Maps FragmentOutput node to the void fragment() shader function body where its inputs become ALBEDO, ALPHA, NORMAL_MAP assignments
Maps Texture2D sampler node to texture(sampler_uniform, UV) GLSL call returning a vec4
Maps the Time node to the built-in TIME float and the UV node to the built-in UV vec2
Maps ColorUniform and FloatUniform nodes to uniform vec4 and uniform float declarations in the generated GLSL
Explains set_shader_parameter() is used to modify uniform values at runtime, working the same for visual or code shaders
Describes the Expression node as a way to write a raw GLSL block with named input ports and one output port inside the visual graph
States that Convert to Text (visual to code) is a one-way operation — the shader cannot be converted back to visual after conversion

evals.name: collision-layer-architecture
evals.prompt: How do I design the collision layer and mask setup for a 2D action game in Godot 4? I have: a player, enemies, player bullets, enemy bullets, environment/walls, and pickup items. What layers do I assign, and what are the mask rules?

assertions.text: Clearly distinguishes collision_layer (the layers a body occupies — what it IS) from collision_mask (the layers a body detects — what it can interact with)
Assigns all six object types (player, enemies, player bullets, enemy bullets, environment, pickups) to distinct dedicated layers
Shows player bullets with a mask that excludes the player who fired them (player bullets only hit world and enemies)
Shows enemy bullets with a mask that excludes enemies (enemy bullets only hit world and player)
Recommends naming layers in Project Settings → Layer Names → 2D Physics before assigning any values
Shows set_collision_layer_value() / set_collision_mask_value() or bit-shift syntax for assigning layers in GDScript code

evals.name: hitbox-hurtbox-layers
evals.prompt: What's the cleanest way to implement hitboxes and hurtboxes in Godot 4 so that player attacks don't accidentally hit the player themselves, enemy attacks don't hit other enemies, I can control exactly which frames deal damage, and the player has invincibility frames after getting hit?

assertions.text: Defines hitbox (the Area2D that deals damage) and hurtbox (the Area2D that receives damage) as separate child nodes from the CharacterBody, each with their own CollisionShape2D
Assigns hitboxes and hurtboxes to dedicated layers separate from the CharacterBody physics layer so friendly-fire exclusion is encoded in the layer/mask system
The hurtbox connects to area_entered signal and pulls the damage value from the hitbox (hitbox exposes get_damage()); the hitbox does not push damage to the hurtbox
The hitbox CollisionShape2D starts disabled by default and is enabled only during the attack animation window (via AnimationPlayer call track or equivalent)
Uses CollisionShape2D.disabled (not Area2D.monitoring) to toggle the hitbox/hurtbox active state — disabling the shape prevents stale contact registration
Implements i-frames by disabling the hurtbox CollisionShape2D for a duration so the player is physically unable to receive damage

evals.name: signals-vs-direct-calls
evals.prompt: In Godot 4, when should I use signals vs direct method calls vs autoloads for cross-system communication? I'm building an inventory system that needs to update the HUD and notify the quest system whenever an item is added or removed.

assertions.text: States the directional rule: signals flow upward and sideways (child notifying parent or sibling systems); method calls flow downward (parent controlling its own child nodes)
Shows the Inventory emitting typed signals (item_added, item_count_changed) without holding any reference to the HUD or QuestSystem
Shows the scene root (Level node that owns all three systems) as the correct node to wire up connect() calls between Inventory, HUD, and QuestSystem in _ready()
Explains autoload event bus as the solution when Inventory and HUD are in different scenes and cannot share a common parent for wiring
Clarifies that direct method calls are correct when a parent controls its own child nodes (intentional, local coupling)
Recommends typed signal parameters so the editor type-checks connections at edit time rather than failing silently at runtime

evals.name: cross-system-communication
evals.prompt: When my player dies in my Godot 4 game, four things need to happen: the HUD lives counter decrements, the camera shakes, all enemies reset to their start positions, and a death jingle plays. What's the cleanest architecture for this, and why?

assertions.text: Player emits a player_died signal and does NOT hold direct references to HUD, CameraController, EnemyManager, or AudioManager
The scene root (Level) connects the player_died signal and dispatches to each of the four systems — it is the only node permitted to know about all systems
HUD lives counter is updated via the signal connection (not by the player calling HUD methods directly)
AudioManager is an autoload singleton for the death jingle because audio needs to play across scene boundaries without a scene-local reference
Explains why get_node() path-based coupling (/root/Level/HUD) is wrong — it breaks on scene rename/restructure and makes the player aware of scene topology

evals.name: navigation-agent-3d
evals.prompt: I want enemies in my 3D Godot 4 game to chase the player around obstacles using pathfinding. How do I set up NavigationAgent3D correctly, and what are the common mistakes that cause enemies to get stuck or walk through walls?

assertions.text: Names NavigationRegion3D with a NavigationMesh resource as the required walkable-surface definition node
Uses set_target_position() to tell the agent where to go — explicitly avoids or warns against navigate_to() which does not exist in Godot 4
Uses get_next_path_position() every physics frame to get the next waypoint and moves toward that (not the final destination directly)
Enables avoidance_enabled on NavigationAgent3D and connects the velocity_computed signal to apply the avoidance-adjusted velocity, preventing enemies from stacking
Connects the navigation_finished signal and stops or transitions the enemy on arrival
Names agent_height and agent_radius on the NavigationMesh as properties that must match the character to block paths under low ceilings and clear walls correctly

evals.name: navmesh-baking
evals.prompt: My 3D Godot 4 game has procedurally generated terrain. How do I bake a NavigationMesh at runtime after the terrain is ready, handle the async bake so agents don't path before it finishes, and deal with dynamic obstacles that can open or close paths?

assertions.text: Calls bake_navigation_mesh(true) for async/threaded baking on large terrain instead of the synchronous form
Connects bake_finished signal and waits for it before activating agents or calling set_target_position()
Explains geometry_parsed_geometry_type or geometry_source_geometry_mode for controlling which scene geometry is included in the bake
Shows how to restrict the bake to a local AABB or use source groups to limit baking to relevant terrain chunks in open worlds
Distinguishes NavigationObstacle3D avoidance_enabled (real-time steering, no rebake) from permanent surface changes (rebake required)
Explains is_target_reachable() or equivalent check to detect when a path cannot be found and trigger a fallback behavior

evals.name: 2d-lighting-setup
evals.prompt: I want to add dynamic 2D lighting to my top-down Godot 4 game — players holding torches, glowing doors, and areas of darkness that the player illuminates as they move. How do I set this up correctly?

assertions.text: States that CanvasModulate is required to darken the scene and that without it lights have no visible effect (scene defaults to fully lit white ambient)
Configures PointLight2D with texture, texture_scale, energy, and color for the torch effect
Shows shadow_enabled and shadow_filter (PCF5 or equivalent) on PointLight2D for soft shadow casting
Explains LightOccluder2D + OccluderPolygon2D for wall shadow casting, including how to set up per-tile occlusion in TileMap
Explains Light2D.item_cull_mask for keeping UI CanvasLayer fully lit while game world is darkened
States that WorldEnvironment and 3D GI nodes (LightmapGI, SDFGI) have no effect on 2D sprite lighting — 2D uses a separate canvas pipeline

evals.name: 2d-normal-maps
evals.prompt: I added a PointLight2D to my Godot 4 game and assigned a normal map to my Sprite2D, but the sprites still look completely flat — the light doesn't create any depth. What's wrong and how do I fix it?

assertions.text: Identifies the import type being wrong as the most common cause: normal map texture must be imported as 'Normal Map' type in the Import panel, not as Color/sRGB
Explains how to fix it in the Import panel: select the texture, change import type to Normal Map, re-import
Names Sprite2D.normal_map as the property to assign the normal texture (not a separate material property)
Explains PointLight2D.range_height: at 0 the light is coplanar (side-shading only); set to 64–128 for top-down depth shading
Names at least one external tool for generating normal maps from pixel art sprites (Laigter, Sprite Illuminator, AwesomeBump, etc.)
Addresses the AnimatedSprite2D limitation (normal map is per-frame, not a single property) or provides an alternative approach
